newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINNISH ERM LINK ON HOLD UNTIL AFTER POLL - ANALYSTS.
newsitem.headline: FINNISH ERM LINK ON HOLD UNTIL AFTER POLL - ANALYSTS.

text.p: The possible linkage of the markka to the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) is no longer the hottest topic on financial markets and a link is not seen until after the local and European polls on October 20, analysts say.

Three weekends of disappointment have passed since Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen said the time was ripe for a decision whether or not to join the ERM. His remarks sparked speculation of a link, boosted the markka and brought bond yields lower.
With the markka on a strengthening trend, the first opportunity for a link right now has passed, analysts say.
"I would say that the immediate likelihood of (Finland joining) ERM has clearly diminished," Esko Torsti, head of Enskilda market advisory said.
"The government has been doing nothing so long that if the markka still firms much more, they will really be trouble," Merita Bank chief analyst Jukka Lepomaki said.
Recent critical comments about ERM from cabinet ministers Claes Andersson and Arja Alho reinforced views that no link would come before the elections.
"For Alho and Andersson, it is convenient to say that a link would not be good ahead of the elections," said Carlo Erakallio, chief economist at Handelsbanken Finland.
Erakallio repeated his view that the link would come only in November.

Choosing to link the markka to ERM would be logical not only since it may be deemed a criterion for entry to Economic and Monetary Union but also "since it would give the government extra credibility for free," Erakallio said.

However, some economists said that if there were any signs from the EU that ERM would not be a strict criterion, Finland may choose not to join, on the basis of political opposition to ERM and some economic risks related to a different currency regime.
"If more signs come that ERM is not necessarily required, it could be that Finland would even stay out of ERM," said Merita's Lepomaki.
In the meantime, the markka should be kept from strengthening to keep industry happy and to avoid upsetting trade unions, which have not yet taken a view on EMU, some analysts said.

After Bank of Finland governor Sirkka Hamalainen on Monday said that further monetary easing would be of no help for unemployment, the bank was less likely to cut rates to keep the markka from rising, some said.
"It seems (the Bank) has realised that 10 basis point moves cannot stop the markka's trend if it is rising," said Enskilda's Torsti.
"But that does not mean that any rate hike is close," he said, adding he expected rates to remain unchanged at their current low levels for quite some time.
Handelsbanken's Erakallio said the central bank should sell markka for currencies, not only to dampen the strengthening trend but also to accumulate a bigger currency reserve.
"Otherwise we will be heading for a fixed currency regime with a small currency reserve," he said.

The Bank of Finland's foreign exchange reserves stood at 35.3 billion markka last week, clearly less than Finnish monthly foreing exchange market transactions which have varied between 69 and 105 billion markka this year.
The reserves have fallen from 48 billion at the end of last year.
"Surely this (buying currencies) would be accepted in a transition period to ERM," Erakallio said.

A senior foreign exchange strategist at a big U.S. investment bank told Reuters on condition of anonymity that he expected the markka to join ERM before the end of the year at "around 3.00 per mark, which is slightly stronger than I had expected earlier."

"Why, because ... the dollar has been gaining and the Finnish currency, looking at the trade-weighted index, has actually been weakening slightly in the past month or so," he said, adding Finland was still "very competitive".

Finland would not suffer from being the only Nordic country joining EMU in the first wave as long as Sweden plays by the rules, continues to trim its public sector deficit and exercises a disciplined foreign exchange policy, he said.
